Atomic Structure.intro: Atoms are made of protons, neutrons and electrons. Understanding the structure of atoms and how it relates to radioactivity is the foundation of P4.

sections.title: Structure of the Atom
points: Nucleus: protons (positive charge, mass 1) + neutrons (no charge, mass 1)
Electrons: negative charge, mass ~1/2000 — orbit in shells
Atom is neutral: number of protons = number of electrons
Atomic number = number of protons; Mass number = protons + neutrons
Atom is mostly empty space — nucleus is tiny compared to atom size

sections.title: Isotopes and Ions
points: Isotopes — same element, same protons, different neutrons; same chemical properties
Ions — atoms that have gained or lost electrons; have a charge

keyTerms.def: Number of protons in the nucleus — defines the element
Total protons + neutrons in the nucleus
Atoms of the same element with different numbers of neutrons
An atom that has gained or lost electrons — has an electric charge

examTips: Isotopes: same protons (same element), different neutrons (different mass).
Ions: same protons and neutrons, different electrons (charged).
commonMistakes: Saying isotopes have different chemical properties — they have the same chemical properties.
Confusing isotopes (different neutrons) with ions (different electrons).
clozePassages: An atom has a small, dense nucleus containing protons and neutrons, surrounded by electrons in shells. The nucleus is positively charged. Protons have a positive charge of +1. Neutrons have no charge. Electrons have a negative charge of -1 and a negligible mass. The number of protons equals the number of electrons in a neutral atom. The atomic number equals the number of protons.

The mass number of an atom is the total number of protons and neutrons. Isotopes are atoms of the same element with different numbers of neutrons. They have the same chemical properties but different physical properties and different stabilities. Some isotopes are radioactive — they have unstable nuclei that decay spontaneously, emitting radiation. The decay of radioactive isotopes is random and cannot be predicted for individual atoms.

Most of an atom is empty space. The nucleus is approximately 10,000 times smaller than the atom itself. The diameter of an atom is about 10⁻¹⁰ m; the nucleus is about 10⁻¹⁴ m. Despite being so small, the nucleus contains almost all of the atom's mass. This understanding came from Rutherford's gold foil experiment, which showed that most alpha particles passed straight through the foil rather than being deflected.

History of the Atom.intro: Our model of the atom has changed over time as new experimental evidence has emerged. This is a key example of how science works.

sections.title: Development of Atomic Models
numbered: Thomson (1904) — plum pudding: electrons in a positive 'sphere' of charge
Rutherford (1911) — nuclear model: small dense positive nucleus, electrons orbit around it
Bohr (1913) — electrons in fixed circular orbits at specific energy levels
Modern quantum model — electrons in probability clouds (orbitals)

sections.title: Rutherford's Alpha Scattering Experiment
points: Alpha particles fired at a thin gold foil
Most passed straight through (atom is mostly empty space)
Small fraction deflected at large angles (small dense positive nucleus)
Very few bounced back (nucleus is very small)
This DISPROVED the plum pudding model

callout.label: Why it Disproved Plum Pudding
callout.text: The plum pudding model predicted all alpha particles should pass through with small deflections. The large-angle deflections could only be explained by a concentrated positive charge (nucleus).

keyTerms.def: Thomson's model with electrons embedded in a diffuse positive sphere
Rutherford's model with a small dense positive nucleus and orbiting electrons
Positively charged particle (2 protons + 2 neutrons) emitted in radioactive decay

examTips: Rutherford's results: most pass through = mostly empty; large deflection = small dense nucleus.
Scientific models change when new evidence cannot be explained by the existing model.
commonMistakes: Saying Rutherford's experiment confirmed the plum pudding model — it DISPROVED it.
Forgetting to explain what each observation tells us about atomic structure.
clozePassages: The model of the atom has evolved over time as new evidence emerged. Dalton proposed atoms were solid indivisible spheres. Thomson discovered the electron and proposed the plum pudding model with electrons embedded in a positive sphere. Rutherford's gold foil experiment showed the atom has a tiny positive nucleus. Bohr proposed electrons orbit in fixed shells. Modern models treat electrons as probability clouds.

Rutherford's gold foil experiment was crucial in developing the nuclear model of the atom. Most alpha particles passed straight through the gold foil, but some were deflected and a few bounced straight back. This proved the atom is mostly empty space with a tiny, dense, positively charged nucleus. The plum pudding model predicted that all particles would pass through with minimal deflection, so the results were surprising and led to a revolution in atomic theory.

Niels Bohr refined Rutherford's model by proposing that electrons occupy fixed energy levels or shells. Electrons can only exist at specific energies and can move between shells by absorbing or emitting photons of light. When electrons drop to a lower energy level, they emit light of a specific frequency, producing atomic emission spectra. These spectra are unique to each element and can be used to identify elements in distant stars.

Radioactive Decay.intro: Some atomic nuclei are unstable and spontaneously emit radiation. This is radioactive decay — it is random and cannot be controlled.

sections.title: Types of Nuclear Radiation
points: Alpha (α) — 2 protons + 2 neutrons; highly ionising; short range in air; stopped by paper
Beta (β) — fast electron from nucleus; moderately ionising; stopped by a few mm aluminium
Gamma (γ) — electromagnetic wave; weakly ionising; needs thick lead or concrete to absorb

sections.title: Nuclear Equations
points: Alpha decay: mass number decreases by 4, atomic number decreases by 2
Beta decay: mass number unchanged, atomic number increases by 1 (neutron → proton + electron)
Gamma: no change to mass or atomic number — just releases energy

callout.label: Summary Table
callout.text: α: most ionising, least penetrating. γ: least ionising, most penetrating. β: in between. Ionising power and penetrating ability are INVERSELY related.

keyTerms.def: Spontaneous emission of radiation from unstable nuclei — random process
2 protons + 2 neutrons; highly ionising; stopped by paper
High-speed electron from nucleus; stopped by aluminium
Electromagnetic wave from nucleus; needs lead to absorb

examTips: α: most ionising, stopped by paper. β: stopped by aluminium. γ: stopped by lead.
Radioactive decay is random and spontaneous — cannot be affected by temperature, pressure or chemical state.
commonMistakes: Saying beta particles are protons — they are electrons emitted from the nucleus.
Confusing ionising power and penetrating ability — they are inverse.
clozePassages: Radioactive decay occurs when an unstable nucleus emits radiation to become more stable. Alpha decay emits a helium nucleus (2 protons, 2 neutrons) — the mass number decreases by 4 and atomic number by 2. Beta decay emits an electron from the nucleus when a neutron converts to a proton — atomic number increases by 1. Gamma decay emits electromagnetic radiation and causes no change in mass or atomic number.

Alpha (α) particles are helium nuclei with high ionising power but low penetration — stopped by a few centimetres of air or thin paper. Beta (β) particles are fast electrons with medium ionising power — stopped by a few mm of aluminium. Gamma (γ) rays are electromagnetic waves with low ionising power but high penetration — reduced but not stopped by thick lead or concrete. The ionising power is related to how strongly each type interacts with matter.

Nuclear equations show radioactive decay with conservation of mass number and atomic number. In alpha decay: ²³⁸U → ²³⁴Th + ⁴He. In beta decay: ¹⁴C → ¹⁴N + ⁰e (electron). Gamma radiation accompanies alpha and beta decay and carries no charge or mass. Nuclear equations must balance — the total mass number and total atomic number must be the same on both sides of the equation.

Nuclear Radiation.intro: Nuclear radiation can be both harmful and beneficial. Understanding the risks and uses is important for P4.

sections.title: Detecting Radiation
points: Geiger-Muller tube — detects ionising radiation; produces electrical pulse
Photographic film — used in film badges for radiation workers

sections.title: Uses of Radiation
points: Medical imaging: gamma cameras (technetium-99m tracer)
Cancer treatment: gamma radiation targeted at tumours
Sterilisation: gamma kills bacteria in medical equipment
Smoke detectors: alpha source (americium-241) ionises air; fire disrupts ionisation
Thickness gauges: beta used to monitor paper/metal thickness in manufacturing

sections.title: Background Radiation
points: Always present from: rocks (radon gas), cosmic rays, food, medical sources
Must be subtracted from measurements in experiments
UK average: ~2.7 mSv per year

keyTerms.def: Low-level radiation always present from natural and artificial sources
A radioactive substance introduced into the body to track a process
Detector for ionising radiation — produces electrical pulses

examTips: Always subtract background radiation in practical experiments.
Medical tracers must be: gamma (penetrating, can be detected outside body), short half-life.
commonMistakes: Forgetting to subtract background radiation in calculations.
Saying alpha is best for medical tracers — it is too ionising and cannot penetrate tissue.
clozePassages: The three main types of nuclear radiation are alpha, beta, and gamma. Alpha particles are the most ionising but least penetrating. They cause serious damage if the source is inside the body (contamination). Beta particles have intermediate ionising and penetrating properties. Gamma rays are the least ionising but most penetrating. All types of radiation can damage living cells by ionising molecules, potentially causing cancer or cell death.

Radiation can be detected using a Geiger-Müller tube connected to a counter. Each ionising particle entering the tube triggers a brief electrical pulse which is counted. Background radiation is always present and comes from natural sources (cosmic rays, radon gas, rocks, food) and artificial sources (nuclear industry, medical uses). Background radiation must be subtracted when measuring the activity of a radioactive source.

Irradiation is exposure to a radioactive source from outside the body. Contamination is when radioactive material enters the body or gets onto clothing and skin. Contamination is generally more dangerous because the source remains in close contact with tissues for extended periods. Protective measures include wearing lead aprons, keeping distance from sources, minimising exposure time, and wearing protective clothing to prevent contamination.

Half-life.intro: Half-life is the time taken for half of the radioactive nuclei in a sample to decay. It is constant for each radioactive isotope.

sections.title: What is Half-life?
points: Half-life = time for activity (or count rate) to halve
Also = time for half the unstable nuclei to decay
Each half-life: remaining nuclei = previous × 0.5
Can range from fractions of a second to billions of years

callout.label: Method
callout.text: After n half-lives: remaining fraction = (1/2)ⁿ. E.g. after 3 half-lives: 1/2 × 1/2 × 1/2 = 1/8 remains. If initial count = 800 and half-life = 2 years: after 6 years (3 half-lives) → 100 counts.

sections.title: Choosing Isotopes
points: Short half-life: medical uses (decays quickly, less long-term exposure)
Long half-life: long-term power sources (e.g. space probes)
Waste disposal: need to store for many half-lives until activity is safe

keyTerms.def: Time for activity of a radioactive sample to halve (or for half the nuclei to decay)
The number of radioactive decays per second — measured in becquerels (Bq)

examTips: From a graph: read off time when activity halves — that is the half-life.
commonMistakes: Saying after 2 half-lives none remains — after 2 half-lives 1/4 remains.
Confusing half-life (time for activity to halve) with time for all nuclei to decay (never fully zero).
clozePassages: The half-life of a radioactive isotope is the time taken for half of the radioactive nuclei in a sample to decay. It is also the time taken for the activity (count rate) of a source to halve. Half-life is constant for a given isotope and ranges from fractions of a second to billions of years. Radioactive decay is a random process — it is impossible to predict which individual nucleus will decay next, but the average behaviour of large numbers of nuclei is predictable.

The activity of a radioactive source decreases over time following an exponential decay pattern. After one half-life, activity halves. After two half-lives, activity is one quarter of the original. After three half-lives, it is one eighth, and so on. The half-life determines how long a radioactive material remains hazardous. Short-lived isotopes decay quickly to safe levels; long-lived isotopes such as plutonium remain radioactive for thousands of years.

Carbon dating uses the known half-life of carbon-14 (5700 years) to determine the age of organic materials. Living organisms maintain a constant ratio of carbon-14 to carbon-12. After death, the carbon-14 decays without replacement. By measuring the remaining carbon-14, scientists can calculate when the organism died. Uranium-lead dating uses the decay of uranium-238 (half-life 4.5 billion years) to date ancient rocks.

Hazards.intro: Ionising radiation damages living cells and can cause cancer. Safe use of radiation requires understanding and minimising the risks.

sections.title: How Radiation Harms
points: Ionising radiation removes electrons from atoms → forms ions → damage to cells
Can damage DNA → mutations → cancer
High doses: radiation sickness, immediate cell death
Low doses: increased long-term cancer risk

sections.title: Reducing Risk
points: Increasing distance from source — intensity decreases with distance²
Lead shielding — absorbs gamma radiation
Limiting time of exposure
Wearing protective clothing and dosimeters
Handling sources with tongs — avoid direct contact

callout.label: Key Distinction
callout.text: Irradiation = being exposed to radiation from a source outside the body. Contamination = radioactive material on or inside the body (more dangerous — continuous exposure).

keyTerms.def: Exposure to radiation from an external source
Radioactive material on or inside the body — ongoing internal exposure
Removal of electrons from atoms — mechanism of radiation damage

examTips: Contamination is more dangerous than irradiation — source stays with the person.
Alpha is most dangerous if ingested/inhaled (highly ionising inside body) despite being stopped by skin externally.
commonMistakes: Saying alpha is harmless because it's stopped by skin — inside the body it is the most damaging.
Confusing irradiation (external source, can step away) with contamination (source on/in body).
clozePassages: Ionising radiation is hazardous because it can damage DNA in cells, potentially causing mutations that lead to cancer. High doses can cause radiation sickness and death. The risk depends on the type of radiation, the dose received, and whether the source is inside or outside the body. Contamination (radioactive material on or in the body) is especially dangerous as exposure is prolonged. Protective measures include shielding, distance, and limiting exposure time.

Workers who handle radioactive materials are monitored using dosimeters that measure their radiation exposure. Precautions include wearing lead aprons, using remote handling equipment, and spending minimal time near sources. In medical and industrial applications, the benefits of using radiation must be weighed against the risks. Background radiation contributes to our total radiation dose throughout our lives.

The effects of radiation on the body depend on the dose and type of radiation. Low doses increase the long-term risk of cancer. High doses cause immediate cell death, leading to radiation sickness. Alpha particles are most dangerous when inhaled or ingested because they are highly ionising inside body tissues. Beta particles can cause skin burns. Gamma rays can penetrate the body and damage internal organs. Risk is reduced by using the ALARP principle — as low as reasonably practicable.

Nuclear Fission and Fusion.intro: Nuclear fission and fusion are reactions involving the nuclei of atoms that release enormous amounts of energy. Understanding both is essential for P4.

sections.title: Nuclear Fission
points: A large nucleus (e.g. U-235) absorbs a neutron and splits into two smaller nuclei
Releases energy + 2-3 neutrons + gamma radiation
The released neutrons can trigger further fissions — chain reaction
Controlled chain reaction: nuclear power stations
Uncontrolled chain reaction: nuclear weapons

sections.title: Nuclear Power Stations
points: Moderator (water/graphite) slows neutrons down — necessary for fission
Control rods (boron) absorb neutrons — control reaction rate
Coolant carries heat away to generate steam → turbine → generator

sections.title: Nuclear Fusion
points: Two small nuclei (hydrogen isotopes) join together to form a larger nucleus
Releases enormous amounts of energy — powers the Sun
Requires extremely high temperatures (~10⁷ K) to overcome electrostatic repulsion
Not yet achieved commercially — potential future energy source

callout.label: Fusion vs Fission
callout.text: Fission: large nucleus SPLITS (current nuclear power). Fusion: small nuclei JOIN (future, powers stars). Fusion releases more energy per kg and produces no long-lived radioactive waste.

keyTerms.def: A large nucleus splits into smaller nuclei, releasing energy and neutrons
Fission reactions where neutrons from one fission trigger further fissions
Small nuclei join to form a larger one — releases enormous energy
Rods in a reactor that absorb neutrons to control the fission rate

examTips: Fission = SPLITS (uranium). Fusion = JOINS (hydrogen). Both release energy.
Fusion is better but requires impossibly high temperatures — the challenge is containment.
Control rods control rate; moderator slows neutrons.
commonMistakes: Saying fusion is already used in power stations — it is not yet commercially viable.
clozePassages: Nuclear fission is the splitting of a large, unstable nucleus into two smaller nuclei, releasing large amounts of energy and two or three neutrons. These neutrons can cause further fission reactions in a chain reaction. In a nuclear power station, the chain reaction is controlled using control rods that absorb neutrons. The energy released heats water to produce steam, which drives turbines connected to generators.

Nuclear fusion is the joining of two small nuclei to form a larger one, releasing enormous amounts of energy. It is the process that powers the Sun. Fusion requires extremely high temperatures (millions of degrees) to overcome the electrostatic repulsion between nuclei. On Earth, scientists are working on fusion reactors that could provide a clean, virtually unlimited energy source. ITER is an international fusion experiment aiming to demonstrate the feasibility of fusion power.

Nuclear fission and fusion both convert a small amount of mass into a large amount of energy, as described by Einstein's equation E = mc². Fission produces radioactive waste that remains hazardous for thousands of years. Fusion produces much less radioactive waste and uses hydrogen isotopes as fuel, which are abundant. The main challenge for fusion power is maintaining the extremely high temperatures and pressures needed to sustain the reaction in a plasma.
